a.name: Refactoring quality and practice
a.definition: Refactor continuously and behavior‑preservingly, guided by smells; choose appropriate techniques, consider performance/testability, avoid cosmetic‑only churn, and isolate risky changes.

b.name: Tests to drive design and refactoring
b.definition: Use tests (including TDD and doubles) to shape design, document behavior, and enable confident refactoring over time.

a.name: Error handling robustness
a.definition: Failure paths are handled explicitly and errors are surfaced with enough context to act on.

b.name: Error message spelling and grammar
b.definition: Strings emitted on failure are free of typos and grammatical mistakes.

a.name: Testing strategy and layering (pyramid)
a.definition: Adopt a balanced test mix emphasizing fast unit tests, few broad E2E/UI tests, pragmatic coverage, realistic data, limited brittle doubles, and awareness of automation limits.

b.name: Testing mix (pyramid) and fast unit tests
b.definition: Favor many small, fast unit tests; fewer integration/service tests; and minimal E2E/UI tests. Keep tests focused and the suite quick and reliable.

a.name: Small, focused, reviewable change
a.definition: The change is scoped to one concern and is small enough to review carefully.

b.name: Commit message structure
b.definition: Commit messages follow a conventional subject/body structure with an imperative subject line.

a.name: Distributed systems trade‑offs and operational resilience
a.definition: Balance consistency/availability/liveness, choose appropriate conflict resolution, and design for resilience (rollbacks, isolation, hot‑swapping, CAP‑aware choices).

b.name: Resilience, availability, and fault tolerance
b.definition: Systems continue operating under failures and load via redundancy, durability/backup, decomposition with coordinated fault handling, and traffic‑shaping/protection patterns; invariants and recovery are preserved.

a.name: Design for testability
a.definition: Structure code and APIs for easy, reliable testing: small decoupled components, clear seams, state abstraction, and refactoring to preserve/enable testability (including TDD feedback).

b.name: Testing strategy, rigor, and methodology
b.definition: A deliberate testing approach (requirements‑driven, TDD/BDD/ATDD as appropriate) with readable tests, adequate coverage/mix, disciplined techniques, and effective test artifacts/fixtures.

a.name: Tests accompany the change
a.definition: The pull request adds or updates automated tests covering the behaviour it changes.

b.name: Change ships with test coverage
b.definition: New or modified automated tests are included alongside the code change, covering the modified behaviour.

a.name: Behavior‑focused and interaction‑oriented testing
a.definition: Specify observable behavior via public interfaces; prefer tests that mirror real interactions; avoid coupling tests to implementation internals.

b.name: Behavior-focused/user-centric testing
b.definition: Tests validate externally visible, user-relevant behavior and avoid brittle assertions tied to implementation details or pixel fidelity.

a.name: Module and class organization and visibility
a.definition: Define clear module/class boundaries, organize package/crate trees logically, and set appropriate visibility to keep APIs maintainable and evolvable.

b.name: Rust API surface and crate organization
b.definition: Design and organize Rust crates and APIs (modules, constructors, macros, extension traits, feature flags, public surface) for clarity, interop, and idiomatic use.

a.name: Import organization and hygiene
a.definition: Place imports at the top; group/sort consistently; prefer absolute over discouraged relative forms where applicable; avoid wildcard/dot imports; remove unused/duplicate imports; and rename to avoid collisions.

b.name: Import statements: placement, ordering, and grouping
b.definition: Place imports at the top, one per line; group by standard library/third‑party/local with blank lines; apply consistent ordering and formatting across files/modules.

a.name: Testing strategy, rigor, and methodology
a.definition: A deliberate testing approach (requirements‑driven, TDD/BDD/ATDD as appropriate) with readable tests, adequate coverage/mix, disciplined techniques, and effective test artifacts/fixtures.

b.name: Tests to drive design and refactoring
b.definition: Use tests (including TDD and doubles) to shape design, document behavior, and enable confident refactoring over time.

a.name: Static analysis and automated enforcement
a.definition: Use linters/formatters/static analysis in CI to enforce standards, catch smells/issues early, prefer auto‑fixable rules, and avoid disabling checks casually.

b.name: Static analysis with actionable feedback
b.definition: Use static analysis/linting (including advanced analyses) to catch defects and design issues beyond compiler checks; surface prioritized, developer‑actionable findings.

a.name: Design for testability
a.definition: Structure code and APIs for easy, reliable testing: small decoupled components, clear seams, state abstraction, and refactoring to preserve/enable testability (including TDD feedback).

b.name: Tests to drive design and refactoring
b.definition: Use tests (including TDD and doubles) to shape design, document behavior, and enable confident refactoring over time.

a.name: Clear rationale in the description
a.definition: The change description explains why the change is being made, not only what it does.

b.name: Motivation stated for the change
b.definition: The submitted description gives the reason and motivation for the change rather than restating the diff.

a.name: Comments: clear, intentional, and why‑focused
a.definition: Prefer self‑explanatory code; use comments sparingly to capture intent, rationale, trade‑offs, and non‑obvious context. Write clear, useful English, avoid restating the code, and keep comments accurate.

b.name: Commenting strategy and quality
b.definition: Favor self‑explanatory code; comment the what/why and non‑obvious assumptions; keep comments minimal but sufficient, accurate, and maintained.

a.name: Change/commit/PR communication quality
a.definition: Titles and messages clearly summarize what and why, provide sufficient context/rationale, avoid narrating the diff, and scale detail to the change; large CLs are annotated to aid review.

b.name: Change description clarity, completeness, and rationale (commits, PRs, changelogs)
b.definition: Commit/PR messages and changelogs clearly and politely explain what changed and why, include sufficient background/context and links, present a coherent scope, and are concise and useful to reviewers and future readers.

a.name: JS/TS module import/export conventions
a.definition: Prefer named exports (avoid defaults), keep import/require at the top and consolidated per path, avoid exporting directly from an import, and use type‑only exports/re‑exports (e.g., export type) where appropriate to support type‑checking/transpilation.

b.name: JS/TS import and export organization
b.definition: Prefer ES module import syntax over require, adhere to conventions for relative vs absolute imports, place exports after imports, and keep import/export sections ordered by tooling.
